info.name: DB Contest — Core API
info.description:
Auth + account management endpoints for the DB Contest Core API (step 1 & 2 of the architecture plan). Sessions are stored server-side and carried in an HttpOnly cookie set by /auth/login — Postman's cookie jar handles it automatically once you run Login inside this collection.

Folders:
- Auth — login, current session, logout, own password change
- Users (admin) — account management, requires `users.manage`
- Operational — health/readiness/metrics. Reachable only against `go run ./cmd/api` on the host (`make run`), NOT against `make stack-up`: there, the internal listener lives only on the compose network and is not published to the host, by design — the same as production. See that folder's description for how to reach it inside the container.

Run order for a fresh environment: Auth ▸ Login (bootstrap account) → any Users request → Auth ▸ Logout.

variable.description: Public listener. In production this is reached through Caddy; only this path is ever exposed.

Internal listener (metrics, health). Only reachable when the API runs directly on the host (`make run`). With `make stack-up` this port lives on the compose network only and is not published — hitting it from Postman then means either an old orphaned `go run` process on the host (kill it) or nothing at all (connection refused), never the containerized api. See the Operational folder for how to reach it inside the container.
Set this to the one-time password printed by `make bootstrap`.
Populated automatically by Users ▸ Create / Reset password.
Populated automatically by Contests ▸ Create contest.
Populated automatically by Contest content ▸ Add question.
Populated automatically by Participant workspace ▸ Get the workspace (its first tab) and ▸ Open a tab.
A registration of {{contestId}}: the registration_id of a row of Participant monitoring ▸ Participants table.
The id of a revision from Participant monitoring ▸ Participant workspace.

item.name: Auth
item.description: Unauthenticated: Login. Authenticated (session cookie required): Me, Logout, Change password.

request.description:
Authenticates and starts a server-side session. The session token is never returned in the body — it is set as an HttpOnly cookie, which Postman stores and replays automatically on every later request in this collection.

Unknown login and wrong password are indistinguishable (both 401 invalid_credentials) and cost the same time, by design — see docs/ARCHITECTURE.md §7.2.

Responses:
- 200 — `{ user, must_change_password }`. If `must_change_password` is true, every endpoint except /auth/password, /auth/logout and /auth/me will answer 403 `password_change_required` until you call Change password.
- 401 `invalid_credentials`
- 403 `account_blocked`
- 429 `too_many_attempts` — 10/15min per account, 30/15min per address

exec: pm.test('response has user and must_change_password', function () {

request.description:
Replaces the caller's own password. Requires the current password (proof of possession — stops a borrowed unlocked browser from being a permanent takeover). Policy: at least 12 characters, must differ from the current password.

This is the one endpoint reachable while `must_change_password` is still true — it's how a one-time password gets replaced on first sign-in.

Every other session on the account is retired as part of this call, and so is this one: the response clears the session cookie, so log in again with the new password afterwards.

Responses:
- 204 — no body
- 400 `wrong_password` / `weak_password` / `same_password`
- 401 `unauthenticated`

Describes the signed-in account and the exact permission codes its roles grant — useful for building UI that hides what the account may not do.

Responses:
- 200 — `{ id, login, permissions: string[] }`
- 401 `unauthenticated`

Ends the session server-side (not just the cookie) and clears the cookie. Calling it with no session, or twice, is not an error — logging out with a stale cookie is a normal thing for a browser to do.

Responses:
- 204 — no body

item.name: Users (admin)
item.description: Account management. Every route here requires the `users.manage` permission — an installation-wide grant, not scoped to any contest. Run Auth ▸ Login first.

query.description: Matches login, full name or email (case-insensitive substring).

request.description:
Paged account listing.

Responses:
- 200 — `{ items: UserResponse[], total: number }` — `total` counts every match, not just the returned page
- 401 `unauthenticated`
- 403 `forbidden`

Creates an account with a server-generated one-time password. The account is flagged so the first sign-in must replace it — see Auth ▸ Change password.

`roles` are global role codes (`student`, `organizer`, `admin`); omit for a student with no elevated role.

Responses:
- 201 — `{ user, one_time_password }` — the password is shown exactly once and is never retrievable again; a lost one is reset via Users ▸ Reset password
- 400 — malformed body
- 409 `login_taken` / `email_taken`

Responses:
- 200 — `UserResponse`
- 400 `invalid_user_id`
- 404 `not_found`

Changes the descriptive fields only — not status, roles or password.

Responses:
- 204 — no body
- 400 — empty full name / `invalid_user_id`
- 404 `not_found`

Denies access and retires every session the account currently holds — blocking takes effect immediately, not at the next login or whenever an open tab's session happens to expire.

An administrator cannot block their own account (guards against locking yourself out).

Responses:
- 204 — no body
- 400 `cannot_act_on_self`
- 404 `not_found`

Restores access. Sessions retired by the block stay retired — the account signs in again.

Responses:
- 204 — no body
- 404 `not_found`

Issues a fresh one-time password for an account the user can no longer reach, and retires their sessions. Same flag as account creation: the next sign-in must replace it.

Responses:
- 200 — `{ one_time_password }`
- 404 `not_found`

Sets the account's global roles to exactly this set (not a merge). Retires the account's sessions, so a demotion bites on the next request rather than at the next login.

Responses:
- 204 — no body
- 400 — unknown role code / `invalid_user_id`
- 404 `not_found`

Creates an account per row, each with its own one-time password.

Accounts are created by an administrator rather than by self-registration (architecture §7), and a group arrives as a list from the department — one request per student would be thirty round trips and thirty chances to lose one.

Partial success is the honest outcome: a duplicate does not reject the rest, and every row that produced no account comes back in `skipped` with a reason (`login_taken`, `email_taken`, `invalid_row`) and the login exactly as it was given, so the line can be found again in the list it came from.

**The passwords appear here and nowhere else.** They are not stored in clear and cannot be fetched later; a lost one is reset.

At most 500 rows: every row costs an argon2id hash (64 MiB, three passes), so an unbounded list would be a way to spend the server's memory with one request.

If the server runs out of hashing capacity part-way, the import stops rather than failing: the accounts already created come back in `created` with their passwords, the rows not reached are listed by login in `not_imported`, and `stopped` is `sign_in_busy` — send those rows again.

Responses: 200 `{ created[], skipped[], not_imported[], stopped? }` · 400 `invalid_request` (too many rows) · 403 `forbidden`

item.name: Contests
item.description:
The contest constructor. Authorisation is two-level: creating a contest is the installation-wide `contest.create` permission, everything about one contest is scoped to it through `contest_managers`, so an organizer never reaches somebody else's olympiad. A system administrator holds `contest.admin_all` and skips the scope.

Order of work: create → languages → translations → story → questions → answers → publish-check → status.

query.description: participant — what a student would see.
Preferred language, e.g. ro. Overrides Accept-Language.

request.description:
Which contests the caller sees depends on who they are, not on a flag they pass:
- system administrator (`contest.admin_all`) — all of them
- organizer (`contest.create`) — the ones they own or manage
- anybody else — the ones they take part in, plus open ones taking signups

`scope=participant` asks for the student view explicitly, which is how staff preview what a participant sees.

Each item carries one **negotiated** title and the `lang` it was served in (`?lang=`, then `Accept-Language`, then the contest default, then `DEFAULT_LOCALE`).

Responses: 200 `{ items: ContestSummary[], total }` · 401 `unauthenticated`

Creates a draft and makes the caller its **owner** — somebody has to be able to appoint managers from the first moment. A read-only SQL policy is stored at the same time, in the same transaction: a contest with undefined SQL access must not be observable.

Everything but the author is optional; an organizer starts from an empty draft.

Responses: 201 `ContestResponse` · 400 `invalid_request` / `invalid_cidr` · 403 `forbidden`

The staff view: **every** translation, not the negotiated one — they are authoring them, and showing only one would make the others invisible in the editor.

`may_monitor` (only here, not on the writes): whether the caller holds `contest.monitor` on this contest, decided as the `/monitor` routes decide it — the workspace offers its monitoring tab from it.

Responses: 200 `ContestResponse` · 403 `forbidden` (not staff on this contest) · 404 `not_found`

A field left out is left alone. `allowed_cidrs: []` clears the restriction; omitting it keeps it.

Editable up to and including `running`: extending the window after a power cut, or fixing a network range that turned out wrong, is exactly what a running contest needs. What cannot move mid-flight is the **shape** — question mode, timing model, session length — since participants are already answering under it.

Responses: 200 `ContestResponse` · 400 · 409 `not_editable` · 404

Only a draft. Once it was published people could see it, and what they saw is a record — getting rid of one of those is archiving.

Responses: 204 · 409 `not_editable` · 404

Replaces the set of languages the contest is offered in. Exactly one must be the default: 'what do we serve when the requested language is missing' must never be ambiguous.

Codes are checked against the `languages` table — adding a fourth language to the installation is an INSERT there, with no migration and no deploy.

Refused once the contest is running: a language added then would be empty for whoever picked it.

Responses: 204 · 400 `invalid_request` (unknown language, no default) · 409 `not_editable`

Replaces the contest's titles and descriptions. The whole set at once, because the publish gate reasons about the set.

Responses: 204 · 400 · 409 `not_editable`

What still stands between the contest and its participants — **all** of it, so an organizer does not need one round trip per missing translation. Always 200: being asked what is left is not a failure.

Problem codes: `no_languages`, `missing_contest_translation`, `no_story`, `missing_story_translation`, `no_questions`, `single_mode_needs_one_question`, `missing_question_translation`, `missing_choice_label`, `no_reference_answer`, `no_schedule`. Each may name the `lang` and the `question_id` at fault.

Responses: 200 `{ ready, problems[] }`

Moves the contest along its lifecycle: draft → published → running → finished → archived. The only step back is published → draft, and it exists because publishing is how an organizer finds out the gate passes.

The gate runs on **both** the move to `published` and the move to `running`: content stays editable while published, so it has to hold again at the moment participants are let in. Requires `contest.publish`.

Responses: 200 `ContestResponse` · 409 `invalid_transition` · 422 `not_publishable` with the same `problems[]` as publish-check

How much SQL power the contest hands its participants. A contest nobody configured reports the read-only default rather than an error — the absence of a policy must never read as 'no restrictions'.

Responses: 200 `PolicyResponse`

Both the AST validator and the database grants are derived from this one row, so they cannot drift apart.

`writable_tables` must be plain lowercase identifiers, optionally schema-qualified: they become GRANT statements when the game template is built, where they cannot be passed as parameters.

A read-only contest carrying write permissions is refused outright — that is a contradiction, not a policy.

Frozen once the contest is running: participants would otherwise have different powers depending on when they connected.

Responses: 204 · 400 `invalid_request` · 409 `not_editable`

item.name: Contest content
item.description:
The story, the questions and the reference answers. Staff-only: these payloads carry the reference answers, and the participant-facing view is a separate projection rather than this one with a field filtered out.

All of it is frozen once the contest is running — changing a question then would change the task under people already answering it.

request.description: Responses: 200 `{ id, translations, updated_at }` · 404 `story_not_found`

Creates the story on first save — a contest has none until one is written.

The game database is English; this is the narrative around it, and it is what a participant actually reads.

Responses: 200 · 400 `invalid_request` (unknown language) · 409 `not_editable`

In display order, with the authored text and the reference answers.

Responses: 200 `{ items: QuestionResponse[] }`

Appended at the end. `is_visible` defaults to **true**: hiding is the deliberate choice, and a hidden question still scores — working out what is being asked is then part of the puzzle.

`kind`: `text` | `choice` | `final`. A choice question needs at least two `choice_ids`; the submitted answer is one of those identifiers, never a label, so grading does not depend on the language the participant read.

Responses: 201 `QuestionResponse` · 400 · 409 `not_editable`

A question that belongs to another contest reports 404, not 403: permission was granted for **this** contest, and the existence of another one's question is not the caller's business.

Responses: 200 · 404 `question_not_found`

Replaces the question's own fields. Text and answers have their own endpoints.

Changing the options out from under existing reference answers is refused: it would leave answers nobody can submit.

Responses: 200 · 400 · 404 · 409

Closes the gap in the ordering, so positions stay 1..n.

Responses: 204 · 404 · 409

Must name **every** question of the contest, exactly once: a partial list would leave positions duplicated or missing, and the participant's view is built from exactly that order.

Responses: 204 · 400 `invalid_request` (partial list) / `invalid_question_id` · 409

Replaces the authored text. `choices` maps each choice identifier to its label in that language.

Responses: 204 · 400 · 404 · 409

Replaces the accepted answers. Several per question is normal: the game database is English, so a translated story that transliterates a name simply adds another accepted spelling — refusing it would score language rather than detection.

`match_kind`: `exact` | `exact_ci` | `regex`. A regular expression is compiled here, at authoring time: a pattern that fails to compile during a running contest would break grading for everybody who reached that question.

Never returned to a participant, and never written to the audit trail.

Responses: 204 · 400 `invalid_request` (bad pattern, or a choice value that is not one of the options) · 404 · 409

item.name: Contest staff and participants
item.description:
Two different permissions on purpose: running a contest (`contest.edit`) does not include appointing who else may run it (`contest.manage`, the owner's alone), and managing the roster (`participant.manage`) includes neither.

Every appointment and every roster change is written to `audit_log` with who did it and from where.

request.description:
Owner first, whatever their login sorts like.

Responses: 200 `{ items: ManagerResponse[] }`

Owner-only (`contest.manage`). Ownership is **not** handed over here: two owners make 'who may appoint staff' ambiguous, and a transfer should not happen quietly through the staff list.

Responses: 204 · 400 `invalid_request` (unknown role) · 404 `user_not_found` · 409 `owner_immutable`

The owner cannot be removed: a contest with no owner has nobody who may appoint anybody.

Responses: 204 · 404 `manager_not_found` · 409 `owner_immutable`

query.description: Substring of the login or full name.

request.description: Responses: 200 `{ items: ParticipantResponse[], total }`

Logins as well as identifiers, because the practical input is a roster pasted out of a spreadsheet.

Partial success is the honest outcome: one mistyped login must not reject the other three hundred rows. `skipped[]` names each row it could not use and why — `unknown_account`, `already_enrolled` or `account_blocked`.

The contest's network restriction does **not** apply here: it governs where a participant may work from, not where the organizer sits while preparing the roster.

Responses: 200 `{ added, skipped[] }` · 400 · 409 `not_editable` (finished/archived)

Only somebody who never started. Once they have worked on the contest their queries and answers are part of the record, and excluding them is disqualification.

Responses: 204 · 404 `participant_not_found` · 409 `participant_started`

Excludes them while keeping everything they did.

Responses: 204 · 404

query.description: A substring of a login, full name or email, at least 3 characters (shorter always answers with nothing).

request.description:
The picker behind both the staff form and the one-person participant form: type a few characters of a login, a name or an email, get back who might be meant. Not scoped to the contest beyond the `participant.manage` permission the route itself checks — every account in the installation is a candidate for staffing or joining any contest.

Only an active account is offered: a blocked or deleted one can never sign in, so it is left out rather than shown as a candidate that would only fail if chosen.

Responses: 200 `{ items: PersonResponse[] }` · 400 `invalid_request` (query over 100 characters)

A student signing themselves up. Needs no staff permission: whether it is allowed is the contest's own decision.

Refused unless the contest is `open`, published, and past neither its start nor its enrollment deadline. A running contest still accepts signups when the timing is `individual` — each participant's clock starts on their own start, so a latecomer takes nothing from anybody.

The network restriction is checked here, against the address resolved through `TRUSTED_PROXIES` — never a header read from the request. Every refusal is written to `audit_log`: the entry that proves the rule works is the same signal that somebody tried from an outside device.

Responses: 201 `ParticipantResponse` · 403 `address_not_allowed` · 409 `enrollment_closed` / `already_enrolled` · 404

item.name: Participant workspace
item.description:
The signed-in participant's own notes and SQL editor tabs on the play screen, stored per registration and autosaved by the interface. Sign in as a participant of `{{contestId}}` first; nobody else can change a workspace. It is not private: whoever holds `contest.monitor` on the contest (its owner, its managers, installation administrators) reads it and its history through "Participant monitoring", and every save of the notes or a tab also records a revision (at most two a minute per document) and every tab created, renamed or closed an event.

Every route is admitted like the rest of `/play`: `403 not_a_participant` / `address_not_allowed`, `409 contest_not_running` / `contest_finished`. The workspace closes with the contest: once it has ended for the participant, reads and writes alike get those same answers, and there is no read-only mode. None of the routes starts an individual participant's clock.

Writes (everything but GET) share one budget of 60 a minute per participant, refused writes included, spent before anything is looked up: past it `429 workspace_too_often` with `Retry-After`. They do not spend the read budget the SQL console shares.

Limits: notes 20000 characters, 10 tabs, titles 1-40 characters without control characters, a tab body as long as a query (64 KiB).

request.description:
Notes and tabs in order. A participant with no tab yet gets one created, named in the request's language (`?lang=` or `Accept-Language`, within the contest's languages): "Query 1", "Запрос 1", "Interogare 1". `notes.updated_at` is null until the notes are first saved. Every `updated_at` on the workspace routes is RFC 3339 with the fractional seconds the database keeps (e.g. `2026-09-17T10:00:00.123456Z`): clients compare it for equality as the document's version.

Spends the participant's read budget (`429 query_too_often`), not the write budget.

Responses: 200 · 400 `invalid_contest_id` · 403 · 409 · 429

Replaces the notes; the last write wins. `body` is required.

Responses: 200 `{updated_at}` · 400 `workspace_notes_too_long` / `workspace_text_invalid` / `invalid_request` · 409 · 429 `workspace_too_often`

Appends an empty tab. Without `title` the server names it "Query N" (in the request's language) with the smallest N no tab uses. Send `{}` for a server-named tab.

Responses: 201 `{id, title, body, position, updated_at}` · 400 `workspace_title_invalid` · 409 `workspace_tab_limit` · 429

Renames the tab, replaces its text, or both; an absent field is left as it is, and at least one is required. Another participant's tab is a 404 like one that does not exist.

Responses: 200 `{updated_at}` · 400 `invalid_tab_id` / `workspace_title_invalid` / `workspace_tab_too_long` / `workspace_text_invalid` / `invalid_request` · 404 `workspace_tab_not_found` · 409 · 429

Removes the tab and closes the gap in positions. The only tab cannot be removed.

Responses: 204 · 400 `invalid_tab_id` · 404 `workspace_tab_not_found` · 409 `workspace_last_tab` · 429

The order after dragging. Must name **every** tab of the workspace exactly once; positions are rewritten 0..n-1 in one transaction.

Responses: 204 · 400 `workspace_order_mismatch` / `invalid_tab_id` · 409 · 429

item.name: Participant signals
item.description:
What the play screen reports about its own participant's browser (design §2.2): leaving the page (the tab hidden or the window unfocused) and pasting into the SQL editor, an answer or the notes. The organiser sees them as signals, not proof: the browser may lie or stay silent.

Admitted like the rest of `/play`: `403 not_a_participant` / `address_not_allowed`, `409 contest_not_running` / `contest_finished`. Its own budget of 12 batches a minute per account, refused batches included, spent before anything is looked up: past it `429 signals_too_often` with `Retry-After`. It spends neither the read budget nor the workspace's.

request.description:
A batch of at most 50 events, in a body of at most 256 KiB. Each event is `{kind, client_at, ...payload}`:

- `page_left`: `away_ms`, from 1 s (shorter absences are not recorded) to 24 h (longer ones are capped);
- `paste`: `target` (`editor`, `answer` or `notes`), `chars`, `text` (its first 500 characters are kept).

Consecutive identical pastes (same target, text and length) are stored as one carrying `count`, and a batch stores at most 10 pastes after that; the rest are dropped. `X-Signals-Kept` counts the events stored.

The server stamps its own time; `client_at` (RFC 3339) is kept only as the browser's claim, and ignored when more than 24 h from the server's clock. An event that cannot be read, of another kind, or out of bounds is dropped and the rest of the batch is still stored: `X-Signals-Kept` says how many were.

Responses: 204 · 400 `signals_batch_too_large` / `invalid_request` / `invalid_contest_id` · 403 · 409 · 429 `signals_too_often`

item.name: Participant monitoring
item.description:
What a contest's participants did, for its staff (design `docs/superpowers/specs/2026-09-18-participant-monitoring-design.md` §4). Behind `contest.monitor` on the contest in the URL — the owner, the managers and installation administrators — and a read budget of 240 a minute per account, refused reads included: past it `429 monitor_too_often` with `Retry-After`. A registration in the URL must belong to this contest; another contest's is the same `404 monitor_participant_not_found` as one that does not exist.

Viewing a participant's feed, queries or workspace is itself recorded in the audit trail (`contest.monitor_view`, at most once per 15 minutes per organiser and participant), and every CSV export always is (`contest.monitor_export`).

request.description:
Every participant of the contest with their counters — queries (all, failed, rejected, from how many addresses), answers (correct, wrong), absences (how many, for how long), pastes, address changes, parallel sessions, last activity — and the six flags of design §5: `multiple_ips` (more than one address), `parallel_sessions` (at least one), `long_absence` (more than 5 minutes away in total or more than 10 absences), `answer_without_queries` (a correct answer with no successful query since the previous answer), `large_paste` (more than 200 characters into the editor or an answer), `identical_queries` (a successful query of at least 60 normalised characters another participant also ran). Hints, not verdicts.

One computation serves every organiser for 3 seconds. At most 2000 rows; `truncated` says there were more.

Responses: 200 · 401 · 403 · 429 `monitor_too_often`

Who the participant is: login, name, status, when their clock started and finished.

Responses: 200 · 404 `monitor_participant_not_found` (another contest's registration, or none) · 401 · 403 · 429 `monitor_too_often`

The feed of one participant, with the same parameters as the contest feed (`participant` aside).

Responses: 200 · 400 `monitor_invalid_cursor` / `monitor_invalid_filter` · 404 `monitor_participant_not_found` (another contest's registration, or none) · 401 · 403 · 429 `monitor_too_often`

The participant's SQL queries, newest first, each whole: the statement, status, error (PostgreSQL's own words and the policy's refusals; a failure of the platform itself is withheld), duration, rows, time and the address it came from. `status` (`ok`, `error`, `timeout`, `rejected`, `running`), `q` (a substring, without case; at most 200 characters; `%` and `_` are text), `cursor` (the last item's, for the next page), `limit` (at most 50).

Responses: 200 · 400 `monitor_invalid_cursor` / `monitor_invalid_filter` · 404 `monitor_participant_not_found` (another contest's registration, or none) · 401 · 403 · 429 `monitor_too_often`

Every attempt, grouped by question, with the queries that led to it: those after the participant's previous answer to any question (or from the beginning) and before this one. At most 100 queries per attempt, each cut to 1000 characters; `more_queries` counts the rest.

Responses: 200 · 404 `monitor_participant_not_found` (another contest's registration, or none) · 401 · 403 · 429 `monitor_too_often`

The notes and SQL tabs as they are now, and the list of their revisions (newest first, without bodies: id, document — `notes` or a tab's id — title, first and last save, size). Looking creates nothing.

Responses: 200 · 404 `monitor_participant_not_found` (another contest's registration, or none) · 401 · 403 · 429 `monitor_too_often`

One revision of the notes or a tab, whole.

Responses: 200 · 404 `monitor_revision_not_found` · 404 `monitor_participant_not_found` (another contest's registration, or none) · 401 · 403 · 429 `monitor_too_often`

The feed as a file, oldest first: `at, kind, login, full_name, registration_id, data` (the item's details as JSON). Streamed as a merge of every source read once; at most 200,000 rows and 64 MiB, with a last `truncated` line when either binds, and at most a minute. A file that stops for any other reason ends with an `incomplete` line. One export at a time per account. Every export is recorded in the audit trail (`contest.monitor_export`) before the file starts. A cell that would start a spreadsheet formula is prefixed with an apostrophe.

Responses: 200 · 401 · 403 · 429 `monitor_too_often` (the budget, or an export already running)

The feed as a file, oldest first: `at, kind, login, full_name, registration_id, data` (the item's details as JSON). Streamed as a merge of every source read once; at most 200,000 rows and 64 MiB, with a last `truncated` line when either binds, and at most a minute. A file that stops for any other reason ends with an `incomplete` line. One export at a time per account. Every export is recorded in the audit trail (`contest.monitor_export`) before the file starts. A cell that would start a spreadsheet formula is prefixed with an apostrophe.

Responses: 200 · 404 `monitor_participant_not_found` · 401 · 403 · 429 `monitor_too_often` (the budget, or an export already running)

item.name: My profile

request.description:
The four numbers of the signed-in account's profile: how many contests it is registered in, how many of them it finished, how many queries it has ever run and how many questions it has ever answered correctly. Counted in one read.

Responses: 200 · 401 · 429 `profile_too_often`

Every contest the signed-in account is registered in, newest first, with its title in the negotiated language, its status and window, the caller's own standing on the roster, and `over` — whether it has ended for this participant.

`result` is present only for a contest that is over: `points`, `solved`, `penalty` (ICPC only), and the table's `state`. `place` and `participants` come only with `place_open`, which is true only when the table is open (final, or a freeze an organiser revealed): the profile does not walk round a freeze. A contest still running carries no result at all — during one, the profile shows nothing of what is happening inside it.

At most 50 contests; `truncated` says there were more.

Responses: 200 · 401 · 429 `profile_too_often`

The result of one finished contest of the caller's: their own standing (and their place, only where the table is open), when their clock started, how long they worked, how many queries they ran and how many succeeded, and question by question the attempts, whether it was solved, when, and what it earned.

Responses: 200 · 401 · 404 `profile_contest_not_found` · 429 `profile_too_often`

The caller's own SQL queries in that contest, newest first, each whole: the statement, status, duration, rows and time. The address is deliberately not here — it is the participant's own and explains nothing to them — and the error text is reduced the way the play screen's own log reduces it: the SQL validator's refusals are shown, the database's own words are not.

`status` (`ok`, `error`, `timeout`, `rejected`, `running`), `q` (a substring, without case; at most 200 characters; `%` and `_` are text), `cursor` (the last item's, for the next page), `limit` (at most 50).

Responses: 200 · 400 `profile_invalid_cursor` / `profile_invalid_filter` · 401 · 404 `profile_contest_not_found` · 429 `profile_too_often`

Every attempt the caller made in that contest, by question, with the queries that led to each — the same read a contest's staff make of the same registration, with the queries under it reduced to what the participant's own log shows.

Responses: 200 · 401 · 404 `profile_contest_not_found` · 429 `profile_too_often`

The caller's notes and SQL tabs as the contest left them. Deliberately without the revision history: how somebody worked is a monitoring fact and the organiser's tool, not a record the participant is offered back.

Responses: 200 · 401 · 404 `profile_contest_not_found` · 429 `profile_too_often`

The caller's whole query log in that contest as a file — the same file they could take during it, by the same writer and the same bounds. Streamed row by row; a file cut at a bound says so in its last line. One download per account at a time: a second while the first is running is `429 profile_too_often`.

Responses: 200 `text/csv` · 401 · 404 `profile_contest_not_found` · 429 `profile_too_often`

item.description:
What a participant is shown of their own account (design `docs/superpowers/specs/2026-09-21-participant-profile-design.md` §3). Behind authentication and nothing else — no `contest.monitor`, no `contest.view`: taking part in a contest is a registration, and these routes answer "what did I do".

The registration is always resolved from the session, so no request can name anybody else's — there is no identifier for one in any of these URLs. Every route under `{{contestId}}` also requires that the contest has ended for this participant: the contest finished, their own deadline passed under an individual timer, or their registration is finished or disqualified. A contest that does not exist, one somebody else is on, and one still running for the caller are all the same `404 profile_contest_not_found`.

A read budget of 120 a minute per account, refused reads included, spent before any lookup: past it `429 profile_too_often` with `Retry-After`. Reading one's own profile is not access to anybody else's data, so none of it is recorded in the audit trail.

item.name: Audit trail
item.description:
Who did what, from where and when — the record required by the specification (§13) and kept for a year.

Written in the same transaction as the action it describes, so an action and its entry land together or neither does. Append-only: there is no route here that writes, and entries never arrive over HTTP.

Behind `audit.view` and nothing else. The trail names who blocked whom and from which address, so reading it is a privilege rather than a side effect of being signed in.

query.description: UUID of the account that acted.
Exact action code, e.g. user.block, contest.status_change.
The thing acted upon; use with entity.

request.description:
Newest first, paged. Every filter narrows an index the table already carries.

The actor comes back as a login rather than an identifier, because a page of UUIDs answers nothing. It is empty for a system event, and for an account deleted since — the trail outlives the people in it, which is the point of keeping one.

A malformed `actor` or timestamp is refused rather than ignored: answering a question about one person with the whole trail is the opposite of what was asked.

Passwords, hashes and tokens never reach the payload — they are stripped at any depth before the entry is written.

Responses: 200 `{ items: AuditEntry[], total }` · 400 `invalid_request` · 403 `forbidden`

item.name: Operational
item.description:
Served on the internal listener ({{internalUrl}}), which is never published through the reverse proxy — by design, so metrics and readiness details are never reachable from the network. No authentication: these exist for the container runtime and Prometheus.

How to actually reach it, depending on how the service is running:
- `make run` (bare `go run ./cmd/api` on the host) — {{internalUrl}} works directly, exactly as configured below.
- `make stack-up` — the port is intentionally not published to the host. Use `docker exec db-contest-api-1 /usr/local/bin/api -healthcheck` for a pass/fail liveness check, or `docker compose --profile observability up -d` and view Grafana/Prometheus, which reach the container over the compose network.
- `make dev-up` (dev overlay, API still run via `make run` on the host) — same as the first case.

If a request in this folder returns core-db failed while `make stack-up` is what's running, you are very likely hitting a leftover `go run ./cmd/api` process still bound to port 9090 on the host from an earlier session — check with `lsof -nP -iTCP:9090 -sTCP:LISTEN` and kill it.

request.description:
Reports only that the process is running — it never checks dependencies, so a database outage does not trigger a restart loop.

Response: 200 — `{ status: "ok" }`

Probes PostgreSQL and the cache concurrently under a shared timeout and reports whether this instance can serve traffic. Failure details are logged, never returned in the body — this endpoint is reachable from the network and driver errors carry hosts and credentials.

Responses:
- 200 — `{ status: "ok", checks: { "core-db": "ok", cache: "ok" }, cache: "memory"|"redis" }`
- 503 — `status: "unavailable"`, same shape, with the failing check(s) marked `failed`

Prometheus scrape endpoint. Only present when METRICS_BACKEND=prometheus (the default) — with the `log` or `none` backend this route does not exist and answers 404, on purpose: serving an empty page would tell a scraper the service is instrumented when its numbers live elsewhere.

Response: 200 — text/plain Prometheus exposition format.

Public, unauthenticated. Reports the build version stamped at compile time.

Response: 200 — `{ version: string }`
